Discover-Tech's online ads — often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods — reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said. Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur. Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume. MALICIOUS ADS SHOWN IN HUNDREDS OF SENSITIVE NETWORKS Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements — called cookie matching — allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned. Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for [USN:L1N2RU186 TEXT:"allegedly supplying spyware"] that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics. Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment. Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads. "You go to almost any site in Palestine — any site — you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said. Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia (NVDA.O) , Sandisk (SNDK.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) , and Micron (MU.O) , as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified. In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf. MEASURES AGAINST DISCOVER-TECH TAKEN Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market. Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies." IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations. Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment. Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been [USN:L6N4240BC TEXT:"targeted using location data"] harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since [USN:L6N44V02G TEXT:"disabled ad tracking"] on some devices.

item.title: Seven subpoenas engulf Nevada election chief in key midterm battle
item.description: As the Trump administration escalates its efforts to compel states to hand over voter rolls in search of fraud, the federal pressure is shaping a high-stakes rematch for Cisco Aguilar's job in Nevada, a top electoral battleground.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff
item.content:encoded: The first Justice Department subpoena demanding voter information caught Democratic Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar off guard. It was June, and his office had been working informally with the FBI on routine [USN:L1N3XI0J6 TEXT:"election security"]. Weeks later, in a July 16 address from the Oval Office, President Donald Trump claimed without evidence that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens had registered to vote, citing an administration review. That review cited Nevada - a key prize in November's fight for control of the US Congress - as one of four states where noncitizen voter registration was widespread. “We're going to be the target of this," Aguilar recalled telling Republican Governor Joe Lombardo before Trump’s address. Then three more subpoenas seeking voter data arrived on September 1 and 2. In total, the Justice Department would deliver seven subpoenas to Aguilar’s office between June 16 and September 2, a public records request shows. As the Trump administration [USN:L6N45D0T4 TEXT:"escalates its efforts to compel states to hand over voter rolls "]in search of fraud, the federal pressure is shaping a high-stakes rematch for Aguilar's job in Nevada, a top electoral battleground. As secretary of state, Aguilar is Nevada's chief election officer, responsible for overseeing elections and certifying results among other administrative duties. The subpoenas have buried Aguilar in paperwork, distracting him from his own reelection campaign against Republican Jim Marchant, who falsely claims the 2020 election was rigged to favor Democrats and [USN:O8N31I01I TEXT:"whom Aguilar narrowly beat in 2022"]. Lombardo has not endorsed either candidate, and did not respond to a request for comment on whom he's supporting. Trump has framed many of his election-related moves as an effort to help Republicans win seats in a year in which his party is widely expected to lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate. He has claimed without evidence that Democrats want noncitizens to be able to vote because their support would return them to power, a charge rejected by Democrats. More than 50 election officials and election-law experts see multiple ways the Trump administration could potentially interfere with the 2026 midterms , Reuters reported on Wednesday. They identified potential flashpoints ranging from election-fraud claims and pressure on state officials to seizures of election materials and immigration enforcement near polling sites. The White House says the administration's goal is to safeguard election integrity and voting security. AGUILAR KEPT BUSY ANSWERING SUBPOENAS Aguilar said he considers the flood of subpoenas a deliberate attempt by the Trump administration to weaken his reelection bid and influence who will oversee Nevada's ballots in the 2028 presidential election. A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency does not confirm or comment on grand jury subpoenas and declined to address Aguilar's assertions about political motivation. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Aguilar said his days were consumed by reassuring worried staff, pushing back on Trump's claims in media appearances, meetings with his personal lawyers and answering the subpoenas. Some donors had withdrawn support because they worried that support could harm their businesses, and his time for fundraising calls has dropped from as many as three hours a day to one a week, he said. “If they can take me out in ‘26, they have control in ‘28,” said Aguilar, one of only two Democratic incumbent secretaries of state running in battleground states this cycle. “It’s absolutely intentional,” he told Reuters in an interview. No other Democratic secretary of state - including in Arizona, the other battleground state where the incumbent is up for reelection - is known to have received any subpoenas, according to the Democratic Association of Secretaries of State and other secretaries in key swing states. Unlike in states like Arizona where counties have more power, Nevada's elections process gives the secretary of state more control in administering elections, Aguilar and other secretaries of state said. NO EVIDENCE OF WIDESPREAD VOTER FRAUD Marchant welcomed the federal spotlight, arguing it would lead voters to question Aguilar's stewardship. "People are so tired of not trusting their election system," Marchant said in an interview, claiming without evidence that Aguilar has overseen elections rife with fraud. Aguilar dismisses such assertions. He pointed out that it was already illegal for noncitizens to vote in Nevada, as is true in all states for federal and state elections. His office had also investigated Trump's claims and has not found evidence that any of the people flagged by his administration were noncitizens, he said. Nevada, whose voter base is roughly 30% Latino, narrowly swung toward Trump in 2024 by 46,000 votes. Louis Jacobson, a senior columnist with the politics website Sabato’s Crystal Ball, moved the race toward Aguilar in September, writing that Marchant's election denialism likely won't be warmly received in a Democratic-friendly political environment. Still, Jacobson told Reuters the Justice Department's focus could cause some voters to stay away from Aguilar if they think he's administered fraudulent elections. It could also elevate him as a defender against Washington overreach. TRUMP'S PRESSURE CAMPAIGN The Trump administration has intensified a campaign to exert control over state elections, even as it struggles in court. The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to provide voter data and has lost 26 of those cases, including against Nevada. The Department of Homeland Security has claimed as many as 16,000 noncitizens are on Nevada's rolls, an effort Aguilar says is designed to intimidate Latino voters who may worry federal immigration agents could seek to detain them at polls. In meetings, DHS officials told Nevada election officials it had thus far confirmed only 185 such cases, according to emails and a video seen by Reuters. Nevada officials, however, said in the emails their records indicated all 185 were citizens and that DHS had provided nothing substantive to suggest otherwise. A DHS spokesperson said officials have since found that at least 2,000 names on the initial list of 16,000 were those of noncitizens. DHS said it had given Nevada enough information to parse the list on their own, but Aguilar said the agency had not yet provided the state with credible evidence. Aguilar said the accusations were meant to exhaust his office and erode public trust. "This whole series of events is like lasagna," he said. "You keep adding on layers of threats and pulling our resources to respond." THE PRICE OF DEFIANCE The pressure has followed Aguilar home and across the state. Publicly, he has tried to project optimism and calm. Aguilar recalled when he served as general counsel to tennis great Andre Agassi's business interests. Agassi had coaches and advisers around him, he said, but when a match began, he alone stepped onto the court. Aguilar said he does not feel as isolated as Agassi did on those occasions, but as Nevada's top election official, he is the final decision-maker and the public face of the state's election system. His initial concern about the subpoenas has now turned into defiance. "Bring it," he said. They "don’t scare me."

item.title: Warsh's quest for quiet Fed gets vocal pushback
item.description: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh’s call for a “quieter” central bank is facing pushback from colleagues who see public communication as a fundamental part of their job and have taken to TV, podcasts, interviews, social media and speakers' podiums to make their policy views known.
item.dc:creator: Ann Saphir, Howard Schneider
item.content:encoded: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh’s call for a “quieter” central bank is facing pushback from colleagues who see public communication as a fundamental part of their job and have taken to TV, podcasts, interviews, social media and speakers' podiums to make their policy views known. Their voices have made a difference, with more than 40 appearances by nearly all of Warsh's colleagues at the central bank convincing traders to scale back rate-hike bets that had mounted after September's rate increase and Warsh's own silence on how much more the Fed may need to do. Data on Wednesday showed consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, shaking up financial markets' Fed expectations yet again. An October rate hike is now seen as a coin toss, an extraordinary lack of clarity that sharpens the focus on the stakes of Warsh's preference for silence. Where the Warsh Fed's communications strategy will settle, however, remains an open question. Warsh speaks in Bangkok on Friday at 0330 GMT (11:30 p.m. ET Thursday) at the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting, a final chance to shape market expectations for the Fed's decision in less than two weeks. At every other opportunity, whether in talks to global central bankers in Sintra, Portugal, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming, or testimony before lawmakers, or answering questions from reporters at the Fed's headquarters, he has argued that the less Fed policymakers say about where they think rates should go, the more markets will be forced to take cues from economic data and make them a better source of information for the Fed as it makes its own rate decisions. He has pared any hint of that so-called forward guidance from the Fed's post-meeting statement, and convened a task force widely expected to recommend jettisoning the rate-path projections produced quarterly that have been a staple of the Fed's communications for years. Other policymakers, however, have been clear they will keep talking, in part because they think it is important for good monetary policy. “If someone wants to present me with an argument that says, not speaking is going to help the public and households and businesses make better decisions and understand the economy, and it's going to help enhance our credibility as an institution, I'm all ears for it,” Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack told Reuters in an interview on Monday. "I think it's a pretty hard argument to make." 'MARKETS TOOK NOTE' Such a shift would mean upending decades of movement away from the cryptic style of Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, which Warsh openly admires. Indeed, US economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, whose pioneering research helped steer the Fed and other central banks toward more frank communications about the monetary policy outlook, this week were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics. Warsh's quiet Fed drive also comes as the Fed is trying to maintain and strengthen its accountability amid White House efforts to influence its monetary policy decisions and challenge its independence. Uncharacteristically pointed remarks from New York Fed President John Williams and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson were particularly effective in resetting rate-hike expectations. "Markets took note of the fact that you had two members of the troika giving a very consistent message," said Richard Clarida, global economic advisor at investment firm PIMCO. The New York Fed chief and the Fed vice chair along with the Fed chair are typically the three most influential policymakers. A former Fed vice chair himself, Clarida said he saw his role back then as communicating the chair's thinking, though he said he could not speak for whether that was still true today. "We're in a regime -- in a world -- where it's important to listen to all of the members of the committee," he said. Speaking in Turkey last week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller gave his own assessment of what will be needed: "additional rate hikes...(that) do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time." Promising an exact rate path would keep the Fed from adjusting as needed to fresh information, Waller said, a risk Warsh has also raised. But giving no signal at all, Waller said, "could surprise markets and create volatility," with investors pricing in a rate hike path that potentially exerts too little or far more restraint on the economy than what Fed policymakers see as necessary. That appeared to have been the backdrop in recent weeks when Williams and Jefferson made the public case against rushing on rate hikes. Markets were expressing a strong conviction for a series of rate hikes at odds with the Fed's September dot plot that showed policymakers expected a less aggressive path. VALUE OF COMMUNICATION That may also have been the situation in August, when markets bet heavily against a near-term rate hike after Warsh declined to offer a detailed rationale for July's decision to hold rates steady despite what he said was a "no tolerance" policy on inflation. That time it was Warsh himself who broke the silence. Even as he repeated his call for a "quieter Fed," he said he wasn't convinced a recent cooling in inflation marked a clear trend -- a signal to markets a rate hike was, indeed, coming. "Transparency about how the central bank is attempting to achieve their objective is important," Charles Evans, a former Chicago Fed president who championed a very strong form of forward guidance to help bolster the economy in the wake of the 2007-2009 financial crisis, told economists in Cleveland earlier this week. Juhi Dhawan, macro strategist for Wellington Management, noted that remarks from Jefferson and Williams may have allowed Warsh to "get his message across without making himself be the conduit for it." "I'm willing to give him some time to find that ideal form of communication," Dhawan said. "I think the value of communication has become apparent, if anything, in the last few months, as the Fed has tried to shift its trajectory on its rate path."

item.title: India says first phase of US trade deal nearly done, insists on edge over rivals
item.description: The first phase of an India-US trade deal is in the final stages of drafting, India's trade minister said on Thursday, but reiterated that New Delhi would proceed only if it secures an advantage over competing exporters.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The first phase of an India-US trade deal is in the final stages of drafting, India's trade minister said on Thursday, but reiterated that New Delhi would proceed only if it secures an advantage over competing exporters. New Delhi and Washington agreed to a framework for the deal in February which brought down to 18% from 50% the punitive tariff on most Indian goods imposed in August last year after a previous round of talks collapsed. Since then, negotiations have run into [USN:L4N45S0BG TEXT:"hurdles"], with officials on both sides signalling that efforts to reach a final agreement have slowed. Indian trade minister Piyush Goyal said the "first tranche" of the deal would be finalised soon. "It's going through the final contours, the legal drafting, and we hope to be able to finalise that soon and operationalise that once we get comparable advantage or competitive advantage over our peer countries," a statement from his office quoted him as saying at an event in New Delhi. Goyal was referring to New Delhi's efforts to secure a tariff advantage for Indian exporters over competing economies such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia in the US market. India wants to ensure its exporters face tariffs no higher than those imposed on competing economies. Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal echoed Goyal's comments. "We anticipate concluding and signing the trade deal at the earliest possible time," Agrawal said, adding that India was seeking preferential market access and greater tariff stability under the proposed agreement. India's goods exports to the United States rose to $42.79 billion in April-August from $40.39 billion a year earlier. In the fiscal year 2025/26, India recorded a trade surplus of nearly $34 billion with the United States. Neither side has publicly detailed the reasons for the delay, but one recent complication has been a new US law that could pave the way for tariffs of up to 100% on Indian goods because of New Delhi's continued purchases of Russian oil. The trade talks have unfolded against a backdrop of increasingly strained ties between India and the United States, complicating efforts to steady their trade partnership. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will [USN:L1N45Z14R TEXT:"visit India"] and Uzbekistan, from October 17 to 22, and will meet government and business leaders to discuss energy cooperation, commercial investment and broader economic ties.

item.title: Portuguese airline deal straps in FOMO premium
item.description: Lisbon chose Lufthansa over Air France-KLM in the battle for state-owned TAP. The implied $5 bln enterprise value looks rich compared with peers. But with few big airlines left to buy, and transatlantic markets booming, fear of missing out helps explain the price tag.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Taslic
item.content:encoded: Deutsche Lufthansa (LHAG.DE) is putting a high-flying valuation on one of Europe’s last big independent flag carriers. The German group on Wednesday [USN:L6N4600RJ TEXT:"beat"] rival Air France-KLM (AIRF.PA) in the race to buy a minority holding in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. The rich proposed price – €1 billion for a 44.9% stake, potentially increasing to €1.2 billion for 49.9% – looks to be driven by a fear of missing out on both healthy transatlantic travel and a dwindling number of viable M&A targets. The process to privatise TAP, which needed a government [USN:L8N2IQ3ET TEXT:"bailout"] during the pandemic, was [USN:S8N3LC0DD TEXT:"relaunched"] last summer after a previous attempt [USN:S8N3LC0DD TEXT:"stalled"]. The plan foresaw the state retaining a majority holding and a 44.9% stake for a private owner, which could rise to 49.9% depending how many employees take up an offered 5% overall shareholding. British Airways owner IAG (ICAG.L) [USN:FWN40K1CZ TEXT:"dropped out"] in April, after its finance chief bemoaned the lack of a “clear path” to majority ownership. Air France-KLM seemed a [USN:L6N40P0ID TEXT:"logical owner"], given its large government shareholders and lack of a southern European hub to complement Paris and Amsterdam. But Lufthansa carried the day with a bid that Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro [USN:L6N4600RJ TEXT:"said"] was 16% higher than Air France-KLM’s. The appeal is clear. With hubs on the western edge of Iberia and strong links into Brazil, TAP enjoyed a 12% share of seats between Europe and South America last year, according to Cirium data. That gives Lufthansa a leg-up into a [USN:L6N3X90TD TEXT:"booming aviation market"] dominated by IAG, Air France-KLM and Chile-listed LATAM (LTM.SN) . TAP is also one of the last big independent flag carriers [USN:L6N44Z0JV TEXT:"left to buy"], while operating margins of 6% in 2025 and 9% in 2024 are respectable. Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr also envisages up to €450 million of annual “synergies”, usually meaning cost savings and revenue boosters, which don’t depend on taking full control of TAP. The issue is the valuation. Bernstein analysts wrote last November that €700 million for the stake would be “comparatively rich”. The winning bid has blown far past that – even though the Iran war has dented the sector’s prospects since then. Using €1.2 billion for a 49.9% stake, the implied equity value for TAP is €2.4 billion. Add the airline’s €2.1 billion of net debt as of June, and the enterprise value Lufthansa is paying works out around €4.5 billion. That’s 6.7 times the last 12 months’ of EBITDA to June. For comparison, the average equivalent multiple for IAG, Lufthansa, Air France-KLM and Finnair (FIA1S.HE) is 3.2, according to Visible Alpha. True, the TAP multiple potentially falls to 4.3 after including the full €450 million of synergies after deducting tax at 17%, based on Breakingviews estimates. But that still looks comparatively pricey. There are strategic questions, too. Barclays analysts wrote last week that competition between TAP and Italy’s ITA – another South America-heavy airline, which Lufthansa has exercised an option to take a majority stake in – could present a “challenge”. Still, investors don’t seem too begrudging: shares in Lufthansa fell 2% on Wednesday, only slightly more than Air France-KLM or IAG. Greater South Atlantic weighting could help Lufthansa in the end. But it comes through a haze of FOMO. Follow @Breakingviews on X CONTEXT NEWS Portugal’s government on October 14 picked Deutsche Lufthansa to buy a stake of up to 49.9% in TAP Air Portugal for €1.2 billion. The German airline group beat its rival Air France-KLM. Lufthansa said on October 15 that it expects up to €450 million of synergies from the combination.

item.title: Banks need 'bare metal' recovery in face of AI risks, says BoE's Breeden
item.description: Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden said on Thursday the central bank was working with banks on deep cyber-recovery options, arguing that lenders can no longer assume their defences are impenetrable in the face of AI-enabled cyber attacks.
item.dc:creator: Rae Wee, Phoebe Seers
item.content:encoded: Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden said on Thursday the central bank was working with banks on deep cyber-recovery options, arguing that lenders can no longer assume their defences are impenetrable in the face of AI-enabled cyber attacks. Breeden also warned that AI advancements had reached a level where the technology posed a "systemic risk" to global financial infrastructure. "It's not enough now to assume that the cyber attackers won't get through....We need to be thinking about what are the bare metal recovery options...that we need for the core services, and we need to think about that end-to-end across the financial system," she said at the Institute of International Finance annual meeting in Bangkok. So-called 'bare metal' systems are entirely independent from a bank's main tech set-up and can kick in if primary operating systems are compromised. Banking regulators globally are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, including in Britain where supervisors have been encouraging the largest banks to examine bare metal recovery plans, Reuters [USN:L6N45Z0FI TEXT:"reported"] on Tuesday. Breeden also warned that the risks of larger and more complex cyber attacks had grown due to AI developments. "The basics of cyber hygiene... those are more important than ever," she said. "Cyber is always the thing that I say keeps me up at night. What is the thing that I worry about the most is waking up and one of our most systemically important banks or a bit of core infrastructure has been attacked and is paralysed."

item.title: UK's Healey says banks are key to economy but keeps tax options open
item.description: British finance minister John Healey said banks were central to the country's economic future on Thursday when pressed by reporters about the likelihood of a windfall tax on their bumper profits in his first budget on October 28.
item.dc:creator: David Milliken
item.content:encoded: British finance minister John Healey said banks were central to the country's economic future on Thursday when pressed by reporters about the likelihood of a windfall tax on their bumper profits in his first budget on October 28. Increasing the 3% surcharge for banks on top of standard corporation tax could raise billions of pounds at a time when many lenders have profited from rising interest rates. However, banks argue they are already highly taxed in Britain compared with some other major financial centres and some analysts say higher bank taxes would see them put up charges. "My observation on the banks is that people too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects," Healey told reporters in Bangkok, where he is attending the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting. "That said, I've got decisions to take in the budget and I will," he added, noting that his comments were not intended to be a steer on any intended tax changes. MANY BANKING ANALYSTS HAVE PENCILLED IN TAX RISE Analysts covering British banks have in recent weeks suggested an increase in the surcharge that banks pay on their profits is likely, with both a return to the previous 8% level and a smaller rise of 2-3 percentage points seen as options. The surcharge currently raises just over £1 billion ($1.3 billion) a year. However, bank bosses have grown more confident that they will avoid such increases. The chief executives of two British lenders told Reuters in recent weeks they did not expect any increase after arguing that such a tax hike could curb lending. Trade body UK Finance said in response to Healey's comments that an increase in bank taxes "would weaken the UK's competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth". In an interview with Bloomberg Television, Healey described banks as "a part of the jewel ... in the British economic crown". When asked if higher taxes on banks could be offset by lower capital requirements, he said he would not be drawn into budget speculation. UK MAY NEED HIGHER TAXES TO KEEP DEFICIT REDUCTION ON TRACK This week, the IMF singled out Britain for praise among major advanced economies for starting a process of deficit reduction that aims at balancing non-investment spending with tax revenue by the 2029/30 tax year. Previous governments have struggled to meet similar rules, due to economic shocks and setting only medium-term goals. Healey told reporters on Thursday that he intended to "stay the path" on deficit reduction in his first budget, when higher inflation and a global rise in interest rates are likely to narrow the margin he has for hitting his goals. "I've said from day one and week one – and I have (Prime Minister) Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me – I will meet those fiscal rules," he said. "I want the budget to be a budget that gives a bit of breathing space but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans," Healey added. British government borrowing costs last week hit their highest since 1998 and are greater than in any other major advanced economy. ($1 = 0.7545 pounds)

item.title: Lufthansa setzt bei TAP auf rasche Synergien und schnelle EU-Genehmigung
item.description: Die Lufthansa erhofft sich vom Einstieg bei der portugiesischen Airline TAP rasche Impulse und setzt auf eine vergleichsweise schnelle Genehmigung durch die EU-Wettbewerbshüter. "TAP passt perfekt zu uns", sagte Lufthansa-Chef Carsten Spohr am Donnerstag in einem Investoren-Call. Gleich vom ersten Tag an werde Mehrwert geschaffen - für die Lufthansa-Aktionäre und die TAP-Investoren. Insgesamt verspreche man sich mittelfristig Synergien von bis zu 450 Millionen Euro jährlich, sagte Finanzchef Till Streichert. Der volle Umfang dürfte erst einige Jahre nach Abschluss der Übernahme erreicht sein. Der mit der portugiesischen Regierung verhandelte Deal solle bald unterzeichnet werden. Komplett über die Bühne gehe die Transaktion wohl im ersten Halbjahr 2028.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Die Lufthansa (LHAG.DE) erhofft sich vom Einstieg bei der portugiesischen Airline TAP rasche Impulse und setzt auf eine vergleichsweise schnelle Genehmigung durch die EU-Wettbewerbshüter. "TAP passt perfekt zu uns", sagte Lufthansa-Chef Carsten Spohr am Donnerstag in einem Investoren-Call. Gleich vom ersten Tag an werde Mehrwert geschaffen - für die Lufthansa-Aktionäre und die TAP-Investoren. Insgesamt verspreche man sich mittelfristig Synergien von bis zu 450 Millionen Euro jährlich, sagte Finanzchef Till Streichert. Der volle Umfang dürfte erst einige Jahre nach Abschluss der Übernahme erreicht sein. Der mit der portugiesischen Regierung verhandelte Deal solle bald unterzeichnet werden. Komplett über die Bühne gehe die Transaktion wohl im ersten Halbjahr 2028. Spohr geht davon aus, dass die EU-Kommission allerdings schneller entscheiden dürfte als bei der Lufthansa-Übernahme der italienischen Airline ITA, weil es mit der TAP weniger Überlappungen im Flugbetrieb gebe. Spohr signalisierte, dass er nicht so sehr mit Auflagen rechne wie beim Kauf von ITA. Zudem hätten die Politiker in Europa verstanden, dass es wichtig sei, größere Unternehmen zu bilden, um im internationalen Wettbewerb mithalten zu können. Portugals Regierung hatte der deutschen Airline am Mittwoch den Zuschlag gegeben, sich mit bis zu 49,9 Prozent an der verstaatlichten TAP zu beteiligen. In einem ersten Schritt erhält die Lufthansa 44,9 Prozent - für 1,025 Milliarden Euro. Dieser Anteil könnte auf bis zu 49,9 Prozent steigen - für dann bis zu 1,2 Milliarden Euro. Dies gilt für den Fall, dass die TAP-Belegschaft ihr Bezugsrecht für fünf Prozent am TAP-Kapital nicht ausübt. Im Bieterrennen setzte sich die Lufthansa gegen den Rivalen Air France-KLM (AIRF.PA) durch. PORTUGAL KÖNNTE KÜNFTIG FÜNF PROZENT AN LUFTHANSA HALTEN Portugal will die in der Corona-Krise 2020 verstaatlichte Fluggesellschaft wieder teilprivatisieren und hat den Prozess im Juli 2025 neu gestartet. Künftig soll es auch Gespräche geben über die 50,1 Prozent, die Portugal dann noch an der TAP hält. Wenn die deutsche Airline diesen Anteil wie geplant - etwa im Tausch von Lufthansa-Aktien - auch übernehme, könne der portugiesische Staat mit bis zu fünf Prozent Anteilseigner bei der Lufthansa werden, sagte Streichert. Aber auch schon als Minderheitsaktionär wird die Lufthansa künftig die operative Führung bei TAP übernehmen und darf den Chefposten bestimmen. Für die Lufthansa sind vor allem Verbindungen nach Lateinamerika interessant, insbesondere nach Brasilien, wie Spohr betonte. Lissabon soll als Drehkreuz gestärkt werden und die nationale Identität der Airline TAP wie bei anderen Töchtern der Gruppe gewahrt bleiben. TAP gilt auch wegen ihrer Verbindungen in das portugiesischsprachige Afrika und in die USA als attraktiv. Die Lufthansa hat der Regierung in Lissabon versprochen, das Wachstum von TAP voranzutreiben. So soll die Flotte von zuletzt rund 100 Flugzeugen ausgebaut werden - auf 117 Maschinen bis 2035. Und danach auf 130, wenn der neue Airport in Lissabon in Betrieb ist. Spohr sagte, die TAP sei bereits profitabel und habe vier Jahre in Folge Gewinn eingeflogen - dies sei für Übernahmen der Lufthansa-Gruppe eher ungewöhnlich. Im ersten Halbjahr 2026 beförderte TAP 8,2 Millionen Passagiere und damit so viele wie nie zuvor. Zugleich kletterten die operativen Erlöse auf den Rekordwert von 2,04 Milliarden Euro. Allerdings weitete sich der Nettoverlust im saisonal schwächeren ersten Halbjahr auf 99,2 Millionen Euro aus, was vor allem auf gestiegene Kerosinkosten zurückzuführen war.

item.title: Albania's leader defies calls to resign as student protesters rampage in capital
item.description: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Thursday rejected calls to resign as thousands of student-led protesters smashed windows and fought running battles with riot police firing water cannon and tear gas in the capital.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci, Edward Mcallister
item.content:encoded: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Thursday rejected calls to resign as thousands of student-led protesters smashed windows and fought running battles with riot police firing water cannon and tear gas in the capital. Protesters voiced anger about perceived corruption, the cost and quality of education and a deal to sell off parts of its pristine southern coastline to a luxury resort development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. They demanded Rama's resignation, saying no one had listened to their concerns during a summer of largely peaceful protests over the development. In a written statement to Reuters, Rama rejected calls to quit. "My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward. The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership," he said. RAMA CONDEMNS ATTACKS ON PUBLIC PROPERTY A student who gave her name as Kiara said the cost of living, poor job prospects, and alleged corruption were the main issues. "Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption. You can only find work in your field if you know a guy who knows a guy," she said, her face covered by a mask, like many on the streets on Thursday. The protests, now [USN:L1N4600LQ TEXT:"in their third day"], mark the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who won a fourth term last year, with EU membership at the centre of his campaign. Parliament cancelled its session as the violence erupted again nearby. Rama, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss the rising cost of education, but added: "Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate demands of students." Tirana's streets were littered with burned out garbage bins, shattered bus stops and broken traffic lights. Wafts of tear gas drifted across the centre. Protesters hurled stones at police, who used water cannon to push protesters back. In the central Skanderbeg Square, police hit fleeing protesters with batons as tourists looked on. PROTESTER SAYS THEY ARE NOT BEING HEARD "This government is corrupted, led and governed by a corrupt prime minister," protester Lulzim Tanushi, a lawyer, said. "Since Rama came to power he has abused and ruined people's lives and that is why people are showing their anger — when they were not heard before." The protests follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by the plans to build the resort, which has faced legal challenges. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was [USN:L6N4380FB TEXT:"wrongfully sold for development"]. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors for drug trafficking, charges his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute. AIMING FOR EU ENTRY AS SOON AS 2028 Albania's image has been tarnished over the years by corruption scandals and political analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking, complicating its efforts to join the EU. Along with Montenegro, Albania is currently leading the accession process among Balkan countries and is aiming for entry as early as 2028. "Corruption must be confronted and, as the EU itself has recently reaffirmed, Albania is tackling it as never before," Rama said to Reuters. "Perhaps some forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to succeed as a forerunner for EU membership. But I will not allow violence to derail Albania's European future." A European Union mission to Albania in a statement on X said: "Constructive dialogue is the only way forward." The unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.

item.title: POLL BoE to raise rates to 4% in November, but economists narrowly expect hold from there
item.description: The Bank of England will raise Bank Rate for the first time in more than three years to 4.0% in November, according to a majority of economists polled by Reuters who have reversed course on the likelihood of a rate rise this year due to persistently high inflation.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Bank of England will raise Bank Rate for the first time in more than three years to 4.0% in November, according to a majority of economists polled by Reuters who have reversed course on the likelihood of a rate rise this year due to persistently high inflation. But there is still no majority among central bank watchers, who have been more guarded than financial market traders, for a further rate rise beyond next month. Markets are fully pricing in four quarter-point rate rises by the end of next year. So far, hefty energy price rises stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran that began in late February have not spilled into broader consumer price rises, although inflation has broadly been above the BoE's 2.0% target for more than five years. With the British economy consistently [USN:L8N4610AT TEXT:"beating expectations"], government bond yields on the rise, [USN:L8N45806W TEXT:"inflation"] at 3.1% and forecast to rise to roughly double the target and no sign of the war ending any time soon, most say it is now time to increase borrowing costs. A strong majority – 54 of 63 economists polled between October 12 and 14 – forecast the BoE would raise Bank Rate by 25 basis points next month, which coincides with the central bank's next set of quarterly forecasts. In last month's survey, about 90% of respondents forecast rates to stay on hold for the remainder of the year. Sonali Punhani, UK economist at Bank of America, who recently changed her view from hold to a hike, said: "The bigger pickup in inflation is still ahead of us rather than behind us." "As a central bank, if you are heading towards inflation close to or above 4%, the risk-reward is probably leaning towards the direction of a hike versus a hold and hoping second-round effects don't come in," she said. GOVERNOR HAS HINTED AT RATE RISE While the BoE was one of the first central banks to raise rates in the last cycle, others, including the [USN:L1N452054 TEXT:"European Central Bank"] and [USN:L6N4570XW TEXT:"Federal Reserve"], have already begun to lift borrowing costs. BoE Governor Andrew Bailey, who so far has been reluctant to cast a vote for a rate rise, dropped a clear hint at the [USN:L8N4590W3 TEXT:"last"] Monetary Policy Committee meeting that higher rates were likely on the way. "The conditions are now moving to a place where that rate hike will need to be delivered, at least according to the guidance that Governor Bailey gave," said Dani Stoilova, UK and Europe economist at BNP Paribas. Still, there is no majority view among economists beyond the rate rise expected for November. Nearly half of economists polled, 30 of 61, expected one more rise in the first quarter of 2027. BoE Chief Economist Huw Pill, who has been voting for a rate increase since April, [USN:L1N461041 TEXT:"again pushed back"] on Thursday against market expectations for a series of hikes. British inflation is forecast to average 3.6% this quarter and 3.8% next, and 3.0% for calendar year 2027. Those forecasts were all revised up from 3.3%, 3.2%, 2.5% in last month's poll. Higher inflation expectations have driven a surge in government bond yields around the world in recent months, taking British government borrowing costs to their highest in decades ahead of the October 28 budget from finance minister John Healey. [USN:L1N4610D3 TEXT:"Healey"] should rebuild his depleted headroom against the fiscal rules to about £15-16 billion (£20-21 billion) at this month's budget to keep bond investors onside, according to a majority of economists surveyed. The British economy put in the best growth performance among Group of Seven developed economies in the first half of the year. But economists have made only a modest upward revision to this year's growth forecast to 1.3%, up from 1.1%, but held their 2027 and 2028 forecasts at 1.2% and 1.5%. ([USN:L6N45N0UX TEXT:"Other stories"] from the Reuters global economic poll)

item.title: Cartier-owner Richemont in talks to join bid for diamond giant De Beers, source says
item.description: Cartier-owner Richemont is in talks to join a consortium bidding for De Beers, the diamond miner being sold by Anglo American and valued at about $1 billion, a person familiar with the matter said.
item.dc:creator: Clara Denina, Olivia Kumwenda-Mtambo
item.content:encoded: Cartier-owner Richemont (CFR.S) is in talks to join a consortium bidding for De Beers, the diamond miner being sold by Anglo American (AAL.L) and valued at about $1 billion, a person familiar with the matter said. A deal would give the Swiss luxury goods group greater influence over a key part of its supply chain as the diamond industry emerges from a prolonged downturn. Richemont, which also owns jeweller Van Cleef & Arpels, is discussing joining the Global Diamond Consortium, a group led by former De Beers Chief Executive Gareth Penny, the person told Reuters. Bloomberg News earlier reported the talks, citing people familiar with the matter. Richemont, worth around $113 billion and cash-rich, was not immediately available for comment. Anglo American declined to comment. "We view Richemont's potential participation as strategically meaningful but more about optics and long-term natural diamond category positioning than a financial event," RBC analysts said in a note. Any bid for De Beers, which has been hit by the rise of lab-grown diamonds, would also depend on [USN:L8N43J0T4 TEXT:"Botswana's"] government, which has a first right of refusal, but has yet to say whether it intends to exercise that option. A spokesperson for Botswana's presidency said on Tuesday the government would not comment until a transaction had been concluded and signed. Officials said this summer a deal was likely to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2026. LONG SEARCH FOR A BUYER Anglo put De Beers [USN:S8N41506W TEXT:"up for sale"] in May 2024 as part of a broader restructuring, after falling diamond prices and growing demand for synthetic stones hit the industry. [USN:S8N41506W TEXT:"De Beers"] has mining and exploration operations in Botswana, Namibia, Angola, South Africa and Canada. Its business has suffered in light of the emergence of lab-grown diamonds, which are much cheaper than natural diamonds but have enjoyed global success. Richemont Chairman and controlling shareholder Johann Rupert, who is South African, has in public comments affirmed his commitment to natural diamonds in high-end jewellery for his brands. Richemont would not be the first high-end jewellery company to directly invest in the mines that produce its diamonds. British diamond brand Graff, for example, holds a 14.9% stake in Gem Diamonds (GEMD.L) which owns the Letseng mine in Lesotho. Richemont shares have held up this year and greatly outperformed the struggling luxury sector, supported by the relative strength of jewellery, which consumers see as a store of value. The luxury conglomerate had around €9 billion in net cash at the end of June, according to filings. The Bloomberg report said negotiations were advanced, though there was no guarantee Richemont would join the consortium. US jewellery retailer Signet could also join the bid, Bloomberg said. Signet did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

item.title: India's goods trade deficit widens; focus turns to trade pacts to narrow gap
item.description: India's merchandise trade deficit widened to $30.21 billion in September as the rise in imports outpaced that in exports, though a rise in outbound shipments and trade deals could narrow the balance over coming months.
item.dc:creator: Shivangi Acharya, Manoj Kumar
item.content:encoded: India's merchandise trade deficit (INTRD=ECI) widened to $30.21 billion in September as the rise in imports outpaced that in exports, though a rise in outbound shipments and trade deals could narrow the balance over coming months. The trade gap has widened as Asia's third-largest economy grapples with a prolonged Iran war that has made energy costlier, hurt shipments to the Middle East and battered markets. India raised interest rates earlier this month and announced a raft of measures to support the rupee. India's trade deficit stood at $26.86 billion in August. Merchandise exports rose to $44.40 billion in September from $43.81 billion in the previous month, while imports increased to $74.61 billion from $70.67 billion. Export growth was broad-based, reflecting strength across sectors including petroleum products, meat, dairy, poultry, electronic goods, handicrafts, and engineering goods, Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal told reporters. India is seeking to diversify its export markets, with a trade deal with New Zealand set to take effect next week and its pact with the UK already in force, while a broader agreement with the EU is moving towards implementation. Agrawal said negotiations with the US were moving in the "right direction," with legal work underway. "We anticipate concluding and signing the trade deal at the earliest possible time," Agrawal said, adding that India was seeking preferential market access and greater tariff stability under the proposed agreement. Ties with the US have been rocky this past year over issues including President Donald Trump's repeated claim of brokering an India-Pakistan ceasefire and a US military attack on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers. The US remained the top destination for Indian exports, with goods shipments rising to $50.81 billion in April-September from $45.82 billion a year earlier. India's services exports stood at $36.35 billion in September, and imports at $19.44 billion, trade ministry estimates showed. Overall goods and services exports rose 13.84% year-on-year to $476.20 billion in April-September from a year earlier, while imports increased 15.68% to $551.13 billion, data showed. GOLD IMPORTS FALL Gold imports fell to $1.8 billion from $2.3 billion in August, when imports had rebounded sharply on inventory restocking ahead of the festive season. Gold imports for April-September fell 27.32% year-on-year to $19.27 billion. Export growth in automobiles and resilient services shipments supported India's overall export performance. India's automobile exports rose 22.5% year-on-year to 684,481 vehicles in September, led primarily by a 26.8% jump in two-wheeler shipments to 544,797 units, data released by an auto manufacturers body showed. Passenger vehicle exports, however, fell 2.2%.
