item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Auf dem EU-Gipfel in Brüssel sind kontroverse Meinungen zu den künftigen EU-Finanzen aufeinandergeprallt. Die Vorschläge der EU-Kommission und der irischen EU-Ratspräsidentschaft seien für die Mitgliedstaaten finanziell nicht tragbar, sagte Kanzler Friedrich Merz am Donnerstag in Brüssel. Kein Mitgliedsland könne es sich leisten, Beiträge in diesem Umfang zu zahlen. Der schwedische Ministerpräsident Ulf Kristersson kritisierte, die Vorschläge seien nicht einmal ein Startpunkt für Diskussionen. Sie würden dazu führen, dass die schwedische Überweisung nach Brüssel um 60 Prozent steigen würde, was völlig inakzeptabel sei. Dagegen bezeichnete der litauische Präsident Gitanas Nauseda den irischen Vorschlag als "ausgewogen". Französische Regierungsvertreter warnten davor, dass Kürzungen an dem Finanzansatz für 2028 bis 2034 nötige Investitionen in der EU gefährdeten. Auf dem EU-Gipfel wird nicht mit einer Einigung der 27 EU-Regierungen über den Kompromissvorschlag gerechnet, den die derzeitige irische EU-Ratspräsidentschaft vorgelegt hatte. Strittig ist sowohl die Höhe von mehr als 1,5 Billionen Euro als auch die Frage, in welchen Bereichen die EU-Staaten das Geld ausgeben sollen. Merz verwies auf einen Sondergipfel im November und den EU-Gipfel im Dezember, auf dem die nötige Einstimmigkeit erreicht werden solle. Die Positionen lägen allerdings noch weit auseinander. "Aber wir sollten für die Ratssitzung im Dezember ein paar Oberhemden mehr einpacken als üblicherweise." Merz hatte sich vor dem Gipfel in Brüssel mit anderen Nettozahler-Staaten wie den Niederlanden, Schweden, Finnland, Dänemark und Österreich getroffen, um eine gemeinsame Position abzusprechen. Auch die 17 sogenannten Kohäsionsländer, die mehr Geld aus Brüssel erhalten, als sie in den EU-Haushalt einzahlen, trafen sich in Brüssel und pochten in einer gemeinsamen Stellungnahme auf deutliche Steigerungen. Sie lehnen zudem nationale Rabatte bei der Berechnung nationaler Zahlungen an Brüssel ab. In deutschen Regierungskreisen wurde mit Blick auf die von der EU-Kommission und Frankreich gewünschten neuen EU-Steuern betont, dass man jede Festlegung auf Zahlen oder höhere Unternehmenssteuern strikt ablehnen werde. Es sei völlig illusorisch, durch sogenannte EU-Eigenmittel die Ausgabenwünsche zu finanzieren. "Das Ziel des Kanzlers auf diesem Gipfel ist es, dass sich die Dynamik im Denken ändert: Wir müssen sparen." Ansonsten verliere man die Akzeptanz der Öffentlichkeiten in den EU-Staaten in Zeiten, in denen nationale Haushalte unter Druck stünden. Neben der Debatte über Geld müsse aber verstärkt über Bürokratieabbau gesprochen werden, sagte Merz. Die Bundesregierung kritisiert, dass von den zwölf begonnenen sogenannten Omnibus-Projekten zum Abbau der Regulierung auf EU-Ebene erst zwei verabschiedet worden seien. Deshalb dringe der Kanzler darauf, dass nun auf jedem EU-Gipfel über Themen wie Wettbewerbsfähigkeit und Verteidigung gesprochen werden solle.

item.title: Russia builds major new drone attack base in six weeks, satellite images show
item.description: The site in what was an empty field in Russia's southwestern Rostov region on August 31 has become a complex facility the size of around 126 soccer pitches, satellite imagery shows.
item.dc:creator: Tom Balmforth, Edward Carron
item.content:encoded: The construction of a large drone launch site near Millerovo, Rostov Region, Russia. PLANET LABS/Pleiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/Handout via REUTERS Russia has nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones in just six weeks, according to defence experts and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, in the latest expansion of its attack capability close to Ukraine . The site in what was an empty field in Russia's southwestern Rostov region on August 31 had become a complex facility the size of around 126 soccer pitches by Wednesday, commercial imagery provided by Planet Labs and Airbus showed. The construction coincides with a surge in the use of Russian jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine, which is struggling to intercept the faster weapons that can travel at speeds of up to 600 km per hour. With the full-scale war well into its fifth year, Kyiv expects Russia to further escalate jet drone and missile attacks this winter. Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, said the site in the imagery would be capable of launching the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, Russia's newest types of jet-powered drone. He said the western edge of the facility showed eight platforms for launch rails capable of firing those drones, adding to an existing Russian network of at least 11 fixed launch sites used for drone attacks on Ukraine. "The speed of construction ... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly," Monnik said. Ihor Malchevsky, 69, escapes from a building what went up in flames after it was hit by a Russian jet-powered drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, September 28, 2026. REUTERS/Thomas Peter Smoke rises in the aftermath of a Russian jet-powered drone strike, September 28, 2026. REUTERS/Valentyn Ogirenko A Russian jet powered drone strikes on one of Kyiv's bridges, Ukraine October 2, 2026. REUTERS/Valentyn Ogirenko The site, he added, looked very close to completion and it will be "probably a matter of weeks before (it is) fully operational, if not earlier." A CHALLENGE FOR NATO The construction of the facility coincides with worsening relations between Russia and the NATO military alliance. European governments accuse Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Kaliningrad exclave. Monnik said the combination of industrial production of jet-powered drones, their increasing sophistication and the relative lack of comprehensive counter-drone defences in many NATO countries were a challenge for the West. "This ability to rapidly field an ability to launch large-scale attacks using UAS (unmanned aerial systems) poses a strategic vulnerability for NATO countries," he said. Monnik said the facility may have the potential to fire 100 jet-powered drones or more in 24 hours, although Russia normally fires them in small numbers throughout the day. It would also depend on factors like available supplies and objectives. Rob Jordan, programme director at the London-based RUSI think-tank, said the concrete pads and two possible takeoff rails shown in the imagery looked consistent with launch tracks for Russian Geran drones. "This level of construction in this short a time is impressive," he said. "This shows the relative faith Russia is putting in its deep strike capability – possibly to the detriment of its conventional land forces." Russia's defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the facility and on its jet-powered drone programme more broadly. USE OF JET DRONES SURGES Military analysts say Russia has shifted its drone production capabilities to jet-powered models as Ukraine has struggled to counter them. Russia increased its use of jet-powered drones roughly six-fold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data reported by Reuters last month. Kyiv and the surrounding region were targeted most heavily, the data showed. The jet drones pose a problem because they are too fast for the interceptor drones designed by Ukraine to cheaply intercept their slower, piston-powered predecessors. Kyiv is now scrambling to devise a solution. Overhead imagery of the new facility taken on August 31 pictured a few vehicles in a field but no sign of construction. Imagery taken the following morning showed that work had begun. Satellite imagery shows launch rails being erected at an area where a large drone launch site is under construction, near Millerovo, Rostov Region, Russia, October 11, 2026. 2026 PLANET LABS PBC/Handout via REUTERS Satellite imagery shows launch rails being erected at an area where a large drone launch site is under construction, near Millerovo, Rostov Region, Russia, October 14, 2026. Pleiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/Handout via REUTERS Satellite imagery shows a closeup of ongoing work at a site where a large drone launch site is under construction, near Millerovo, Rostov Region, Russia, October 11, 2026. 2026 PLANET LABS PBC/Handout via REUTERS Satellite imagery shows a closeup of ongoing work at a site where a large drone launch site is under construction, near Millerovo, Rostov Region, Russia, October 14, 2026. Pleiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/Handout via REUTERS The site, which occupies an area of around 0.9 square kilometres, lies about 3.5 km from Russia's Millerovo air base, home to the 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment. According to DroneSec, the new launch site likely sits within the air defence "bubble" provided by systems at the airbase, making Ukrainian attempts to target the new facility more difficult. Of the eight launch platforms, two already had rails on them, a Reuters analysis showed. Rails were being constructed on two other pads as well, while other construction work was visible from space over the course of three days this week.

item.title: Two ships ablaze off Romanian Black Sea coast, 7 sailors missing
item.description: Rescuers were searching for seven missing crew on Thursday from one of two chemical tankers that caught fire overnight just outside Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea, after Russian drones strayed into national airspace, Romanian officials said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Rescuers were searching for seven missing crew on Thursday from one of two chemical tankers that caught fire overnight just outside Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea, after Russian drones strayed into national airspace, Romanian officials said. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, but declined to say whether they were Russian. "Two air drones hit them," Dan told reporters in Brussels ahead of a summit of EU leaders, adding only a few hours had elapsed since the strikes and Romania was waiting for more information. "There will be a reaction from the Romanian state," he added. The two ships hit overnight were both anchored in the Black Sea near the mouth of the Sulina canal leading into the Danube River, a major shipping route used by Ukraine as Russia has attacked Ukraine's own Black Sea ports. One was in Romanian waters, the other just outside. The incidents follow drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring fellow NATO member Bulgaria over the past 10 days. At least 23 sailors were lost from those strikes, which took place just outside NATO's territorial waters. SEARCH FOR MISSING SAILORS Romania's naval authority said it received an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader. Seven of its 12 crew were missing and 5 were rescued. The ship was hit 13 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, one mile outside Romanian waters. The interior ministry said it had sent two Black Hawk helicopters to the search and rescue mission, as well as two ships with medical staff on board. "At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves," it said in a statement. Late on Wednesday, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker [USN:L1N46014H TEXT:"Yara J"] also caught fire, 8-10 miles southeast of Sulina, inside national waters. Romanian authorities initially said it was not clear whether it had been attacked. All its crew were safe. INCREASING ATTACKS ON BLACK SEA SHIPPING Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube. It has reported repeated [USN:L1N46014H TEXT:"breaches"] of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years. Both Wine Trader and Yara J caught fire near the mouth of the Danube River's Sulina Canal leading to the Black Sea, where ships often anchor waiting to pass because of delays from weather and congestion. Both ships were empty of cargo. Increasing attacks on Black Sea shipping connected with the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months have threatened to cause a global food crisis, as both countries are major exporters of grain, as is Romania. "We're looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu told a security conference in Warsaw earlier this week. "It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence." Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said EU leaders would discuss on Thursday a proposed [USN:L8N4610KR TEXT:"moratorium"] on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea. Dan and Radev will meet NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte later on Thursday. Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube River ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania. For its part, Ukraine has targeted Russian ships near the mouth of the Don River in the Azov Sea.

item.title: Nestle India flags food, commodity inflation after profit surges 36%
item.description: Nestle India flagged inflation and rising commodity prices as challenges on Thursday after resilient demand for Maggi instant noodles and Nescafe coffee helped drive a 36% jump in its second-quarter profit.
item.dc:creator: Surbhi Misra, Praveen Paramasivam
item.content:encoded: Nestle India (NEST.NS) flagged inflation and rising commodity prices as challenges on Thursday after resilient demand for Maggi instant noodles and Nescafe coffee helped drive a 36% jump in its second-quarter profit. Consumption tax cuts and selective price increases have supported sales growth for Indian consumer goods makers, even as they face mounting input cost pressures, especially for packaging, edible oils and agricultural commodities. The Indian arm of Switzerland's Nestle (NESN.S) said it is focusing on new and improved products, investing in its brands and managing costs to counter food inflation and higher commodity costs. "Rising inflation, particularly food inflation, is a reality," Chairman and Managing Director Manish Tiwary said, citing "a challenging environment" due in part to higher commodity costs. India's retail inflation (INCPIY=ECI) accelerated to 5.54% in September, data showed on Monday, nearing the upper end of the central bank's tolerance band as war in the Middle East and a weak monsoon pushed up prices. Net profit was 10.27 billion rupees ($108.03 million), while revenue rose 20% to 67.88 billion rupees. Despite the sharp profit increase, earnings were broadly in line with estimates, disappointing investors who had anticipated a stronger beat, Systematix Group analyst Abhishek Mathur said. He added that the market may also be factoring in slower revenue growth in coming quarters. Shares slumped roughly 9% after the results. In the September quarter, sales volume grew at a double-digit pace, with Nestle India citing higher rural penetration for Maggi, sustained growth on quick-commerce platforms and launches under the KitKat and Munch brands. The results also come as India pursues an unprecedented food safety crackdown, including proposed warning labels for packaged foods and nationwide inspections of eateries, as concerns over hygiene and quality intensify. Nestle India did not directly address the developments. Tiwary, however, said: "At Nestle India, food safety and quality are the foundation of consumer trust." ($1 = 95.0625 Indian rupees) (This story has been officially corrected by the brokerage, to change the analyst's name, in paragraph 7.)

item.title: Gold Fields CEO plays down prospect of higher Northern Star offer
item.description: Gold Fields' CEO played down speculation on Thursday that the South African gold producer will raise its offer for Northern Star, saying the Australian miner first needs to acknowledge that it sees a potential path to a tie-up.
item.dc:creator: Melanie Burton
item.content:encoded: Gold Fields' (GFIJ.J) CEO played down speculation on Thursday that the South African gold producer will raise its offer for Northern Star, saying the Australian miner first needs to acknowledge that it sees a potential path to a tie-up. Gold Fields has embarked on a long-planned road show in Australia this month, where CEO Mike Fraser is aiming to boost its profile with investors in the country accounting for around half of its business. Last month, it lobbed a A$38.7 billion ($27.1 billion) buyout proposal in shares and cash for Perth-based Northern Star, Australia's biggest gold miner, in a bid to create the world's second-biggest producer of the yellow metal. But Northern Star [USN:L1N45K003 TEXT:"rebuffed"] that offer. Under pressure from activist investor [USN:L4N4291EG TEXT:"Elliott"] Investment Management following a run of poor performance, it opted instead for its own overhaul plans. Northern Star said in a statement on Thursday that its board remained focused on acting in the best interests of shareholders. "This includes engaging with parties on proposals that represent value above what we believe Northern Star can generate as a standalone company. The Gold Fields proposal was not in that category," it said. Gold Fields' Fraser said the market expected his company to make another offer. "But I think before you get into ... throwing in new offers, you've got to at least have some reciprocation to say, actually we think there is a pathway (to value) here," he told Reuters. "At the moment, we're not hearing any of that." Northern Star’s shares are up 10% since the day before the approach became public. Gold Fields shares have fallen nearly 17% in the same period. FRASER SEEKS TO RALLY INVESTORS BEHIND MERGER PLAN Gold Fields' South African shareholders — among them the Public Investment Corporation, its largest shareholder with a 15% stake — saw the strategic logic of a merger, Fraser said. But he added that some South African investors were concerned about the potential for cost escalation, the delivery of a turnaround plan for Northern Star and the potential for Gold Fields to overpay. PIC has previously said that it did not wish to express a view on a potential merger and did not immediately comment. Meanwhile, Fraser said that, though Australian institutional investors were not overly familiar with Gold Fields' business, after a number of conversations he believed "people buy into the logic of the merger." "What we've heard from investors on both sides is that they see this as being compelling," he said. Gold Fields had also met with Elliott, which has a 6% stake in Northern Star and has previously emphasised its commitment to the gold miner's turnaround. Fraser said Elliott was focused on delivering a short-term outcome, whereas Gold Fields' merger strategy was seeking to "create a story that is actually much more enduring". "They've got an important role, but they're not long-term shareholders," said Fraser. Elliott had no immediate comment. COMBINED COMPANY COULD RERATE, GOLD FIELDS CEO SAYS Gold Fields has said it saw $4 billion to $5 billion in synergies from a tie-up, which come mostly from tax benefits and combining operations. Both miners have gold operations in Western Australia, including around the town of Kalgoorlie where Northern Star runs Australia's biggest gold mine, known as the Super Pit. Fraser said one overlooked benefit, however, was the prospect that a combined company could rerate. "We absolutely believe that this combined business would be trading at a much higher relative multiple than what we're trading at today," he said. Gold Fields' shares are trading on an enterprise multiple of 3.5 to 4 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, much cheaper than Northern Star's multiple of 7 to 8 times. Larger peer Agnico Eagle (AEM.TO) is trading around an 8 times multiple. Fraser said he would walk away if there was no alignment on value creation. "But that's a step away from where we are today," he said.

item.title: Pope Leo had a good night in hospital as he recovers from lung cancer surgery
item.description: Leo's public engagements have been cancelled until October 20.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo had a good night in hospital and has eaten breakfast, the Vatican said on Thursday, as the 71-year-old recovers from surgery for lung cancer. Leo has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung in a surgery on Tuesday afternoon. The Vatican has said the surgery was completed successfully, without complications. It has not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis. Blood tests and a chest X-ray carried out on Wednesday showed normal post-operative results, the Vatican said. US President [USN:L1N46017L TEXT:"Donald Trump"], who has clashed with Leo on a number of issues, added his voice on Wednesday to the global chorus of goodwill for the ailing pope. "I want to see Pope Leo get well," Trump told reporters. "I just want to wish him well, get better fast." Vice President JD Vance, a Catholic convert, also added his prayers. "May God grant him strength as he works to get better. I hope he knows that millions of American Christians are thinking about him," Vance wrote on X. Further updates are expected on Leo's condition on Thursday, but his pathology report may not be available for several days. Leo's public engagements have been cancelled until October 20. The cancer diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"future shape of his papacy"] as he deals with the illness. Leo normally has a packed schedule. He is due to make a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17 and the Vatican press office said on Wednesday that "nothing has changed" regarding the planned trip. However, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said that the dates could change because of the amount of time that Leo's recovery would take.

item.title: Pakistan school roof collapse kills at least 32 children and a teacher
item.description: Rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble of the privately run Al-Khair Education Center, while panicked parents and relatives gathered outside the building seeking news of their loved ones.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: At least 32 schoolchildren and one teacher were killed on Thursday when the roof of a school collapsed during morning classes in the northwestern Pakistani city of Peshawar, police and rescue officials said. Rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble of the privately run Al-Khair Education Center, while panicked parents and relatives gathered outside the building seeking news of their loved ones. Most of the students killed were under 13. At least 45 people suffered major and minor injuries, said Arif Khattak, regional director of the Rescue Department. Television footage showed rescuers clawing through debris with their bare hands and carrying bloodied children to waiting ambulances as relatives and residents crowded the narrow alley where the school stood. A higher-floor roof collapsed onto students in classrooms below, crumpling two storeys of the building, a rescue official said. "The fatalities include 12 girl students and a female teacher," Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Mohammad Asim said. Three children were in critical condition, with head injuries, Asim said, adding that most of the 20 injured brought to that hospital had been treated and sent home. The incident took place at 8:48 a.m. local time (0348 GMT) and the rescue operation lasted for four to five hours, Khattak said. "It was a weak building structure," Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said. "Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, which caused the collapse." Saeed said the school's owner had been arrested and authorities had opened an investigation. DISTRAUGHT RELATIVES DEMAND JUSTICE Distraught relatives accused the school of ignoring concerns about the building's condition and demanded accountability. "Make an example of them, a lesson for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make money without providing facilities," said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse. Earlier, police chief Saeed said he feared the death toll could rise as just 47 of the 110 students in three classrooms at the time had been rescued. There was no immediate comment from school officials. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the tragedy and offered condolences to the victims' families, according to a statement from his office.

item.title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Zelenskiy says 'we're done' with Trump's energy truce
item.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Ukraine's patience had run out.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Flynn, Max Hunder
item.content:encoded: Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday, after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Kyiv was "done" supporting a ceasefire on energy targets announced by US President Donald Trump and ignored by Russia. Since Trump's surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy, Kyiv had suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel prices on global markets. But in the days that followed, Russia rained down deadly missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people. In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's patience had run out. "The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done," he told the newspaper. Zelenskiy also made clear he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX's Starlink receptors this week, which have curbed Ukraine's ability to use them to pilot its drones, were a policy decision. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," he told the FT. In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump, as president of the United States. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote. BIGGEST RIFT WITH WASHINGTON OF THE WAR By effectively walking away from Trump's demand that Ukraine halt attacks on refineries, Zelenskiy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend had "damn well better stop". Trump has long had a testy relationship with Zelenskiy and berated him in the White House in February 2025. But his sharp turn against Kyiv in recent days has little precedent. He first angered Ukraine last week by abruptly lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, and then called on Ukraine to replace Zelenskiy. Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington. Over the past several days, Ukrainian officials have reported that they have not received the usual warnings from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles, which rely on US satellite detectors. Trump has denied withholding intelligence. Zelenskiy said the failure to provide the warnings had been presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch. At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). Ukrainian officials have said that is too slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones. REFINERY SUPPLYING MOSCOW HIT Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia. Trump, under pressure to lower fuel prices, especially for diesel which has reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices. Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia's refinery throughput, helping supply the capital. Regional governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram that a [USN:S8N44O03I TEXT:"major Ukrainian drone attack"] had caused a fire at the refinery. Damage was being assessed and emergency services were at the scene. A Ukrainian official confirmed that Ukraine had hit a Russian refinery overnight in response to Moscow's heavy ballistic missile and drone attacks this week that violated the energy truce. In the latest attacks on Ukraine, three people were killed and six wounded in the central region of Kirovohrad overnight, as Russia launched more than 500 drones. State-owned energy company Naftogaz said a gas extraction facility in Poltava was damaged and operations were suspended. The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was still ongoing to do so. BREAKDOWN IN RELATIONS In the FT interview, Zelenskiy criticised Washington’s eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump’s apparent admiration for Russia's Vladimir Putin. The rift has raised concern in Kyiv and European capitals about the heavy reliance in Ukraine on US intelligence and technology. Under Trump, Washington has already halted weapons supplies to Ukraine while allowing its European allies to continue buying US arms on Kyiv's behalf. But [USN:L6N460199 TEXT:"Europe has no ready-made alternatives"] to Starlink, or to US satellite systems used to detect Russian missile launches. Zelenskiy has said that Ukrainian military officials had been warned by US counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, Zelenskiy told the newspaper he could agree only if in return he were given more US-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the “minimum” that would be acceptable. Ukraine's navy said on Thursday it had destroyed six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region. The navy said on Telegram it used its Neptune coastal missile system in the attack.

item.title: India’s bank privatisation offers cautious win-win
item.description: Canada’s Fairfax is set to acquire 61% of IDBI Bank for $5.6 bln, the largest foreign bet on an Indian lender. For the buyer, it's a cheap valuation and it delivers an okay return for state rescuer LIC. But the deal will test whether New Delhi is really willing to stand back.
item.dc:creator: Ujjaini Dutta
item.content:encoded: After a decade of dithering, New Delhi looks poised to check the privatisation of IDBI Bank (IDBI.NS) off its to-do list. Canada's Fairfax Financial (FFH.TO) is set to buy 61% of the lender for 529 billion rupees ($5.6 billion) in India's largest cross-border bank deal. It offers the buyer’s founder, Prem Watsa, a chance to build a leading private sector institution if the government stays out of his way. It was 2016 when New Delhi first floated the idea of cutting its stake in IDBI from 80% to below 50%. The government and state-controlled Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIFI.NS) will each offload a roughly 30% stake. They’ll partly cash out of the thinly traded and volatile shares at a 10% discount to the last closing price on Wednesday, the day before officials named Prem Watsa’s company as their preferred “strategic buyer”. There’s no binding agreement but if the deal goes through, it'll be a remarkable full circle for a bank that was one of the hardest hit by a nationwide asset quality crisis. Around 2019, IDBI's gross non-performing loans stood at nearly one-third of its portfolio. That prompted the government to nudge LIC to pump in 216 billion rupees, or $2.3 billion at current exchange rates, to raise its 8% stake to 51% in 2019. Today, bad loans are just 2.3% of IDBI’s book. Fairfax looks well placed to build on that repair. It’s paying a multiple of around 1 times IDBI’s trailing book value. A well-run private sector bank with better tech savvy like ICICI Bank (ICBK.NS) commands 2.5 times. Fairfax will combine IDBI with its non-bank lender $1.1 billion IIFL Capital Services (IIFS.NS) and insurer Digit to cross-sell banking, insurance and financial services products. For LIC, the deal crystallises a 7.44% annualised price return on its 2019 investment. That is less than ideal compared to the 10% yielded by India’s benchmark Nifty 50 stock Index (.NSEI) over the period but for New Delhi, it is not a terrible price to pay to stop a bank from going under. The sellers will gain in two more ways. Offloading IDBI will bring some fiscal relief for the government firefighting surging oil prices and help it hit its annual target for divestment for the first time in seven years. They'll also have a chance to improve their returns: LIC and the government will withdraw from the board but retain a combined stake of 34%, higher than the 26% regulatory cap on voting rights Fairfax will be subject to as a private owner of an Indian bank. That offers plenty of upside so long as officials can resist meddling. Follow Ujjaini Dutta on LinkedIn and X . Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings is set to buy 60.7% of India's IDBI Bank for 528.78 billion rupees ($5.56 billion), the Indian government said in a press release on October 14. The government named Fairfax as its preferred strategic buyer but no binding agreements have been signed. If a deal goes through, it would represent the largest foreign direct investment into the financial sector. New Delhi and state-controlled Life Insurance Corp of India will each sell a roughly 30% stake. The government will retain a 15% stake and LIC a 19% stake after the transaction. They will withdraw from the bank's board and become public shareholders. Fairfax will offer 81 rupees per share for IDBI Bank. The price is above the benchmark price of 75.99 rupees per share determined by the government based on fair valuations but a discount of 10% to the closing price of 90.39 rupees on October 14. India first said it would consider cutting its stake in IDBI Bank from around 80% to below 50% in February 2016. LIC started increasing its stake around that time. In 2019, LIC became the majority owner. Around that time, the bank's gross non-performing loans amounted to nearly 30% of its total assets. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Pernod Ricard first quarter sales fall less-than-expected, cautious optimism on China
item.description: Pernod Ricard reported on Thursday a smaller-than-expected 0.9% drop in sales for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, hurt by weak demand and de-stocking in China and the United States although demand in India was strong.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Pernod Ricard (PERP.PA) reported on Thursday a smaller-than-expected 0.9% drop in sales for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, hurt by weak demand and de-stocking in China and the United States although demand in India was strong. Pernod, the world's second-largest spirits maker after Diageo (DGE.L) , said underlying trends in China were improving, confirming its cautious optimism ahead of the Chinese Mid-Autumn Festival. The maker of Martell cognac and Absolut vodka, which held unsuccessful merger talks with Jack Daniel's maker Brown-Forman earlier this year, reiterated a forecast for broadly stable net sales in the fiscal year started on July 1 Pernod reported Q1 sales of €2.234 billion ($2.5 billion), an organic decline of 0.9% against estimates of a 1.7% decline in a company-compiled poll of analysts Shares in the company [USN:L6N4610IR TEXT:"rose around 3%"] following the results. Sales fell 10% in the US and 25% in China but rose 19% in India in the first quarter Finance chief Mauve Croizat told analysts inventory adjustments in China and the US would likely continue through the full year. In China, she said consumers were shifting to more private occasions rather than out-of-home alcohol consumption In India, the group has said it is taking preparatory steps toward a potential initial public offering. It reiterated that the decision to proceed with an IPO remained subject to board approval If approved, the IPO would still take a few months to execute with timing dependent on market conditions, Croizat said Pernod also said it would strongly defend its organic operating margin supported by strict cost control It also reiterated it expected sales growth at the lower end of its 3% to 6% target range through 2029, underscoring the prolonged downturn facing global spirits makers($1 = 0.8917 euros)

item.title: AI credit jitters drive US tech default insurance to record highs
item.description: The cost of insuring against US tech defaults hit record highs on Thursday, in the latest sign of credit stress building in the AI trade, especially for data centres that are dependent on future revenue.
item.dc:creator: Tom Westbrook, Amanda Cooper
item.content:encoded: The cost of insuring against US tech defaults hit record highs on Thursday, in the latest sign of credit stress building in the AI trade, especially for data centres that are dependent on future revenue. Hotter-than-expected [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US inflation data"], together with mounting expectations for higher interest rates, are colliding with concern about how quickly massive investment in artificial intelligence will translate into profits, as well as whether heavily indebted companies can generate returns fast enough to service mounting interest costs. Credit default swaps (CDS) are sending a warning signal to markets. Five-year credit default swap spreads at cloud computing giant Oracle (ORCL.N) were quoted at 288 basis points on Thursday by S&P Global Market Intelligence. They were unchanged from the previous close, but up from 260 bps a week earlier. Five-year spreads for AI investor SoftBank (9984.T) widened 24 bps to 424 bps. Data-centre operator CoreWeave's CDS (CRWV.O) have blown out past 1,000 bps, S&P LSEG data showed . The loss-making "neocloud" company that owes nearly $50 billion, according to LSEG data, is in the eye of the storm. Its debt prices are tumbling, with 2032 paper changing hands at around 78 cents on the dollar, for a yield of just over 16%, on the Tradeweb platform. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade’s canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. "Its bonds have sold off sharply ... this is a sign that investors might be going off the AI investment narrative, which has included massive debt issuance to fund AI ambitions." A surge in quarterly revenue from [USN:L6N4601AA TEXT:"AI developer Anthropic"] did little to calm the market's nerves. According to an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting with the company's leadership in San Francisco on Wednesday, third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter. Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $2 trillion. DEBT MARKET JITTERS CDS spreads show the number of basis points charged for default protection. The greater the perceived risk of a credit event, the wider the spread, meaning the 1,000 bps for CoreWeave CDS implies a risk of default in the coming five years of nearly 63%, up from around 30% a year ago. Earlier this week, [USN:L1N45Z07U TEXT:"Broadcom Chief Executive"] Hock Tan compared the investor rush for anything AI-related to "casino gambling." CoreWeave stock was down another 6.8% in early premarket trading on Thursday, following a 15% slide during regular hours on Wednesday that was followed by a 6% drop in after-hours trading, which has vaporised around a fifth of the company's value. CoreWeave shares have fallen over 8% this year, while those of rival Nebius (NBIS.O) , for which there are no publicly tradable CDS, are up about 120%. Credit default swap spreads for Amazon (AMZN.O) , Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Meta (META.O) , and Nvidia (NVDA.O) also traded at record highs, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though they have risen far more slowly than Oracle, or CoreWeave.

item.title: EU leaders kick off summit with wrangles over high energy prices and spending
item.description: The European Union began a packed summit on Thursday that quickly underscored wrangles over how to tame soaring energy prices, design a budget to keep the bloc competitive and curb surging exports from China that are blamed for job losses.
item.dc:creator: Philip Blenkinsop, Kate Abnett
item.content:encoded: The European Union began a packed summit on Thursday that quickly underscored wrangles over how to tame soaring energy prices, design a budget to keep the bloc competitive and curb surging exports from China that are blamed for job losses. The leaders from the EU's 27 members met in Brussels on the back of securing an [USN:L6N45V0LF TEXT:"agreement with Beijing"] to limit imports of hybrid cars from China, a first step towards cutting a goods trade deficit that hit €360 billion ($400 billion) in 2025. The summit takes place at a time of heightened economic anxiety, with fuel price spikes since the Iran war putting cash-strapped governments on the back foot, companies struggling and Europe wanting to shore up its defences and [USN:L6N4610BB TEXT:"support Ukraine"]. The clock is also ticking on a series of elections in Europe over the coming months including in France in April, which could propel French [USN:L8N4601WM TEXT:"far-right leader Marine Le Pen"] to the presidency vowing to slash her country's contribution to the EU budget. Slumping in the polls at home, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters that positions were still far apart on the budget, which has pitted net contributors such as Germany against net beneficiaries. The latest proposal would safeguard subsidies for farmers and regions, which critics say sucks money away from more urgent areas to keep up with the US and China. "We are, therefore, facing very, very difficult negotiations," Merz said. MERZ SAYS FROZEN RUSSIAN ASSETS MUST STAY IN EUROPE Merz also gave a [USN:L6N4610ML TEXT:"pointed rebuff"] to a proposal by the United States, reported in the Financial Times, for European countries to unfreeze some Russian sovereign assets immobilised after the invasion of Ukraine . The idea would be to transfer them to a vehicle overseen by Washington in an attempt to revive peace talks, the FT reported, citing people briefed on the matter. "These are assets that are frozen in Europe, and they should remain frozen in Europe. This is our affair, and we are the ones who decide on it," Merz said. While France is also a net contributor to the EU budget, its officials warned that a blunt focus on spending cuts would be counterproductive, hobbling measures that were also intended to make the bloc more competitive. "We can clearly see that cuts alone cannot resolve the equation," one official said. Draft conclusions from the summit indicate leaders want the Commission to continue talks with Beijing, while also making full use of EU trade defence measures and adding new trade instruments to protect the bloc further. "These imbalances are not limited to one sector. We don't have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost," said a senior EU diplomat. Beijing has said that hyping up the issue of economic imbalances is an excuse to promote protectionism and exert pressure on and restrict China. "We don't have enough measures to counter unfair practices, we have also not invested enough in our own competitiveness and innovation, the new EU budget will need to be equipped for that," Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten told reporters. GERMANY'S U-TURN ON CHINA IMPORTS [USN:L6N45R0Q0 TEXT:"Franco-German proposals"] released last week are also likely to be the focus of discussions. The EU's two largest economies said there was an urgent need for measures to deal with imports of chemicals and PET — the plastic widely used in packaging — and called for measures to retaliate quickly against countries that harm the bloc. The paper marks a sharp turn for Germany, which only two years ago was the most vocal critic of EU anti-subsidy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. Several EU countries have also put high energy prices on the agenda. One area of contention is the wish by countries including the Czech Republic and Italy [USN:L1N45L09G TEXT:"to weaken or suspend"] the EU Emissions Trading System, a regulation forcing power plants and industries to buy CO2 permits when they pollute. The prime ministers of Finland, Sweden and Denmark hit back in a letter praising the system as a driver of energy security by helping Europe reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels. They warned "any weakening" would hinder investment in clean industries. One of Friday's main topics will be the challenges facing Ukraine, with President [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:"Volodymyr Zelenskiy"] due to attend at a time when Kyiv is at [USN:L8N4600M6 TEXT:"loggerheads with the US"] over intelligence sharing while missiles and drones hammer Ukrainian cities. Leaders are expected to discuss Ukraine's funding needs for 2027, with Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs comparing the cost to each citizen of the price of a beer. "It is one beer less for one European a year. We can afford that. But Ukraine needs it now," he said. ($1 = €0.8991)

item.title: Gold climbs over 1% on softer dollar, yields ahead of US inflation data
item.description: Gold prices climbed more than 1% on Thursday as the dollar and US Treasury yields remained under pressure, while investors looked to fresh US inflation data for clues on whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again this month.
item.dc:creator: Sherin Sans
item.content:encoded: Gold prices climbed more than 1% on Thursday as the dollar and US Treasury yields remained under pressure, while investors looked to fresh US inflation data for clues on whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again this month. Spot gold was up 1.3% to $4,156.58 per ounce by 1124 GMT. US gold futures for December delivery rose 1.7% to $4,178.50 per ounce. The dollar (.DXY) slipped 0.5%, making greenback-priced bullion more affordable for holders of other currencies, while the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield also fell to a three-week low. "Falling real yields and resilient investment demand help gold recover from its post-CPI selloff, but the technical outlook remains fragile," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US consumer prices"] accelerated in September on a surge in gasoline costs, with price pressures spreading beyond energy and raising concerns among economists that underlying inflation could be getting sticky. Market participants are now awaiting Producer Price Index (PPI) and retail sales data due at 1230 GMT for further clues on inflation trends and the Federal Reserve's policy path. "If the PPI comes in as expected, which is 5.4% year on year, then that pattern will be continued. So you would expect bond yields to rise again. We're just going to have to watch it very carefully," said Rhona O'Connell, head of market analysis at Stone X. Traders are pricing in about a 29% chance of a rate hike later this month, compared with 22% before the data, according to CME's FedWatch Tool . Gold is traditionally seen as a hedge against inflation, but higher interest rates make the non-yielding asset less attractive. San Francisco Fed President [USN:L6N4601E8 TEXT:"Mary Daly"] said further rate increases would probably be needed, but signalled no need to act at the October meeting; Vice Chair for Supervision [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"Michelle Bowman"] said there was time to wait. Among other metals, spot silver gained 1.9% to $56.69 per ounce, platinum rose 0.7% to $1,617.50 per ounce and palladium climbed 3.5% to $1,132 per ounce.

item.title: Firmus CEO's Aussie scapegoating has iota of truth
item.description: Oliver Curtis blamed his neocloud's failed $5 bln IPO on local buyers' dim views of risk-taking. Investors Down Under can be cautious. But the deal was over-hyped and valuation punchy, not to mention Firmus and its banks all failed to play to the market Curtis is blaming.
item.dc:creator: Antony Currie
item.content:encoded: Oliver Curtis has taken the blame game over Firmus Technologies' [USN:L6N45V00W TEXT:"IPO flop"] to a new level. Rather than acknowledging fault, or singling out the investment bankers or the punchy $30 billion valuation they sought, the co-CEO of the neocloud company pointed the finger squarely at his native country Australia for having "dim views of people taking a risk". The self-styled "homegrown hero" is not alone. Down Under billionaire and Firmus shareholder James Packer lamented that the country "tends to tear down aggressive entrepreneurs and America builds them up". While these sound like typical throwing-toys-out-of-the-pram moments, both have a point, albeit a small one: The breadth of Australia's $2 trillion economy is a concern. Industries like car manufacturing and steelmaking have disappeared or shrunk. The country fell 10 places in the decade to 2024 to rank 74th on Harvard's Economic Complexity Index; of the OECD countries, only Chile has a lower score. Mining and banking account for around 60% of the domestic stock market capitalisation. Yet that ignores the growing financial and existential fears about AI that have now spread to Firmus' US rival CoreWeave (CRWV.O) : on Wednesday its shares slumped 15% and its bonds due in 2032 traded below 80 cents on the dollar. Moreover, Firmus had heaps of red flags too, the biggest being backer Coatue Management cutting its IPO commitment by 90% to $100 million last week, the AFR reported. Those factors would have understandably scared off the country's pension, or superannuation, funds that manage A$4.8 trillion ($3.3 trillion) of assets. While they have a reputation for being risk-averse, they have readily backed scrappy mining startups and fintech firms and some have ploughed money into unlisted data centre outfits like AirTrunk and CDC Data Centres. They have also been crying out for decent-sized IPOs. Firmus would have been the biggest ASX listing this millennium by almost 40%. It's not as if Curtis, who a decade ago was jailed for insider trading, or his bankers - Bank of America, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley and Morgans Financial - were blissfully unaware of these conflicting dynamics. Yet they still tried to garner an IPO valuation triple Firmus' worth in an August funding round for a company with a minuscule track record, little revenue and a convicted criminal in the C-suite. If Curtis wants to revisit an IPO any time soon - perhaps on the Nasdaq - he'd better start dining on some humble pie. Follow Antony Currie on Bluesky and LinkedIn . Firmus Technologies co-founder and co-CEO Oliver Curtis said that the failure of the neocloud company's IPO was "a missed opportunity for Australia, to be brutally honest". He made the comments on October 11 to Liam Mendes, a reporter from The Australian newspaper who tracked him down on the way to a meeting in Singapore. Curtis also said: "It's about Australia understanding ultimately we should be a homegrown hero, manufacture amazing technology with an amazing pipeline of opportunity...it is disappointing that Australia decided that there was a mantra of disbelief...Australia will, generally, take dim views on people taking a risk." Australian billionaire and Firmus investor James Packer echoed Curtis' comments on October 13, telling The Australian that "Australia tends to tear down aggressive entrepreneurs and America builds them up." item.title: Dollar eases from 18-month high as Treasury yields fall; Fed hike bets ease
item.description: The dollar slipped from an 18-month peak on Thursday as a sharp drop in Treasury yields weighed on the greenback, while cautious remarks from Federal Reserve officials tempered October hike expectations despite hot inflation data.
item.dc:creator: Sophie Kiderlin
item.content:encoded: The dollar slipped from an 18-month peak on Thursday as a sharp drop in Treasury yields weighed on the greenback, while cautious remarks from Federal Reserve officials tempered October hike expectations despite hot inflation data. The dollar index , which measures the US currency against a basket of peers, was last down 0.2% on the day at 102.03, having hit an 18-month high on Wednesday after US inflation figures came in stronger than expected. That helped the euro bounce 0.5% from an 18-month trough to $1.1216, putting it on track for its biggest daily gain in nearly two months. Sterling strengthened 0.5% to $1.3253, remaining broadly steady after data showed that [USN:L8N4610AT TEXT:"Britain's economy unexpectedly grew"] 0.1% in August. Markets turned [USN:L6N46100A TEXT:"cautious"] and trading became somewhat choppy as Wednesday's [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"hot US CPI reading"] initially bolstered bets on higher-for-longer Fed rates, and worries about AI companies' heavy debt burdens were revived, driving safe-haven flows into Treasuries. The rally in US government bonds pushed the benchmark 10-year yield to 5.085% while the 30-year yield fell to 5.428%, both at around three-week lows. As well as the moves in bond yields and jittery equities, with tech stocks especially taking a hit, Kit Juckes, chief FX strategist at Societe Generale, also noted that shifts in positioning played a role in the dollar's moves. "The overall picture is I think one of a little bit of a tug of war between people who would like to look for a correction in the dollar. Because positioning's too big, we've come a long way, there's not really much new news, we've got a lot of rate hikes priced in and so on. And then the economic data, which can flip it," he said. "I suspect it'll be choppy and uncomfortable until we've got past the retail sales and PPI numbers." Both data points are due later in the day, with producer prices expected to show a jump in business costs last month. Market pricing for an October Fed rate hike [USN:L6N4600VL TEXT:"rose sharply"] to 50% on the back of the CPI data, before a chorus of Fed officials – including Vice Chair for Supervision [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"Michelle Bowman"] and San Francisco Fed President [USN:L6N4601E8 TEXT:"Mary Daly"] – said the central bank could wait for a clearer picture ahead of the October 27 and 28 meeting, tempering those bets. "Despite the whole CPI number coming slightly stronger than expected, I think markets have sort of taken the view that maybe it was not hot enough to force the Fed's hand for October," said Khoon Goh, the head of Asia research at ANZ. "(The) October (meeting) is also just a few days before the midterm elections as well," he added. "And that's possibly why the market doesn't want to be more aggressive in pricing in for October." Investors will also watch remarks from Fed officials including Chair Kevin Warsh at IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday for clues on the US central bank's next move. The Australian dollar fetched $0.6919 , down 0.7%, after [USN:L1N46100L TEXT:"local employment"] unexpectedly slid in September, while the Japanese yen strengthened to 157.80 per dollar.

item.title: Oil prices slips as US weighs easing sanctions on 'shadow fleet'
item.description: Brent crude prices fell over 1% on Thursday as potential US steps to ease restrictions on Russia's "shadow fleet" tankers soothed price concerns, but attacks on ships in the Middle East and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure limited the decline.
item.dc:creator: Ahmad Ghaddar
item.content:encoded: Brent crude prices fell over 1% on Thursday as potential US steps to ease restrictions on Russia's "shadow fleet" tankers soothed price concerns, but attacks on ships in the Middle East and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure limited the decline. The international benchmark lost $1.15, or 1.1%, to $104.91 a barrel by 1157 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up marginally by 31 cents, or 0.3%, to $95.40, amid expectations for a large draw in weekly inventories. Oil prices fell after a US official said on Wednesday that the US administration was considering [USN:L1N46017R TEXT:"easing sanctions"] on some of Russia's unregulated tankers, a move that could help lower freight rates and increase flexibility in diesel shipments, PVM Oil analyst John Evans said. The discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, to ease a surge in prices globally. The new talks centre on Washington potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. Prices, however, were still finding support from an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis and renewed attacks on ships in the region. A [USN:L1N4600JW TEXT:"container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank"] near the strait after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday. Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. "The ongoing conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is keeping a geopolitical premium in oil markets, but energy infrastructure has not been attacked in the last several days," MUFG analysts said in a note. Meanwhile, [USN:L6N4610BB TEXT:"Ukraine resumed its attacks"] on Russian refineries with a strike on a plant in the Ryazan region, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy voiced anger at a "dangerous" withdrawal of US intelligence. Spain will [USN:L6N4610OA TEXT:"release"] 4.4 million barrels from strategic reserves in October, an Energy Ministry official said on Thursday, as the International Energy Agency began a meeting expected to clarify details of a 100 million-barrel oil stock release, including diesel, with the timing and scale of the move in focus. item.title: TSMC 'prudent' going into 2027 after posting sixth straight quarter of record profit
item.description: TSMC, the world's largest manufacturer of advanced chips, struck a note of caution for 2027 on Thursday due to macroeconomic uncertainties, tempering an otherwise upbeat outlook after reporting a sixth consecutive record quarterly profit on robust AI-driven demand.
item.dc:creator: Wen-Yee Lee, Ben Blanchard
item.content:encoded: TSMC, the world's largest manufacturer of advanced chips, struck a note of caution for 2027 on Thursday due to macroeconomic uncertainties, tempering an otherwise upbeat outlook after reporting a sixth consecutive record quarterly profit on robust AI-driven demand. While Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) (2330.TW) said demand was "extremely robust" and it sees no sign of a slowdown in what it calls the AI mega trend, the company was being cautious in its business planning. "Looking ahead, we continue to observe consumer and price-sensitive end-markets segments are being challenged due to the impact of rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties," Chief Executive C.C. Wei said on an earnings call. "As such, we are being prudent in our business planning going into 2027." However, it reiterated that demand far exceeds its supply capacity, with the expectation that its 2026 full-year revenue grows by about 44%, up from a previous forecast of greater than 40% last quarter. The company also said the emergence of agentic AI central processing units and continued demand for networking chips would drive future silicon demand. STOCK SHOCK TSMC's results come amid concerns that the AI investment surge is losing momentum. On Wednesday, [USN:L6N4600AA TEXT:"ASML"] (ASML.AS) , the world's largest maker of tools used to make AI chips and advanced semiconductors, provided an upbeat outlook. TSMC, a key supplier to Nvidia (NVDA.O) and Apple (AAPL.O) , said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by as much as 61% from a year earlier to $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. It maintained its capital spending expectation for 2026 at $60 billion to $64 billion. TSMC's Taipei-listed shares closed down 2% ahead of the earnings release, in line with a broader tech [USN:L6N46104Y TEXT:"sell-off"] amid worries that more interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve could pummel shares of AI stocks that are sensitive to higher borrowing costs. Shares of South Korean rivals Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK Hynix (000660.KS) slid more than 10%. Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments, which owns TSMC stock, said the company's remarks reflected the caution expressed by many semiconductor companies during recent earnings releases and investor days. "The key risk is that TSMC's caution translates into broader earnings downgrades across a value chain accustomed to sustained upward revisions, but for now, this looks like sensible expectation management rather than a change in the sector's long-term fundamentals," he added. Analysts say demand for TSMC's AI chipmaking capacity, as well as its advanced chip packaging technology, CoWoS, remains strong. That has catapulted Asia's most valuable company to new heights. Its market capitalisation is almost double that of Samsung Electronics at around $2 trillion. TSMC said net profit in the July-to-September quarter hit T$763.1 billion ($23.59 billion), up 69% from a year earlier and beating a T$746.3 billion LSEG SmartEstimate compiled from 16 analysts. The result was TSMC's highest-ever quarterly net income, as well as its 11th consecutive quarter of profit growth. Last week, it reported a 50% year-on-year rise in [USN:L6N45U0AF TEXT:"third-quarter revenue"], beating market forecasts and hitting a new record. TEXAS EVALUATION TSMC is investing $265 billion to build chip factories in the US state of Arizona, including an additional $100 billion that was unveiled in July. It said its second fab in Arizona has completed construction, with mass production scheduled to begin in the third quarter of 2027, ahead of schedule. In September, Reuters reported that TSMC was [USN:L6N45M06T TEXT:"evaluating"] a potential investment in Texas. Wei said the company was studying expansion opportunities outside Arizona as major US customers have asked TSMC to increase its local manufacturing capacity, adding that the US government has been supportive. "Texas is one," Wei said. "We sent teams to Texas to do all the evaluation." Tesla CEO Elon Musk also said last week that his companies would build and operate the Terafab AI chip complex, with TSMC potentially subleasing a part of it. Wei said TSMC had discussions with Terafab, but stressed that any fab collaboration would have to be operated by TSMC. [USN:L6N4600AA TEXT:"ASML"] (ASML.AS) said on Wednesday customers were already looking to place orders for 2029 and 2030, easing concerns that the AI investment boom was losing momentum. TSMC's Taipei-listed shares have gained 57% so far this year, in line with a 62% rise for the broader Taiwanese market. ($1 = 32.3450 Taiwan dollars)

item.title: BofA's mega-fine blunted by Team Trump history
item.description: A $1.2 bln penalty over compliance issues often rattles bank boards and shareholders. Just ask erstwhile CEOs of Citi, TD and Wells Fargo. Boss Brian Moynihan's money-laundering mess leaves him in comparatively tepid water, given the administration's vexing signals on wrongdoing.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Gandel
item.content:encoded: Aesop's "Boy Who Cried Wolf" will be a treasured tale for Bank of America (BAC.N) CEO Brian Moynihan. The mega-lender he runs just copped to violating the Bank Secrecy Act with a deficient anti-money-laundering program, transgressions that include a $1.2 billion fine. Compliance matters of this magnitude tend to unnerve boards and shareholders, but the Trump administration's past pronouncements on financial wrongdoing dilute the moral of this particular story. The US Treasury Department and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency unveiled enforcement action on Tuesday, accusing BofA of failing to report more than $5 billion of suspicious transactions in a timely manner. The agencies levied one of their biggest-ever penalties because, they said, Moynihan and his team put revenue ahead of addressing concerns raised by regulators before. BofA said it is [USN:O8N43T02A TEXT:""far along with and committed to completing""] the related issues and already absorbed many of the costs, including hundreds of millions of dollars during the third quarter. Moynihan has some damage control to do, but he may be in relatively tepid water compared to erstwhile counterparts. Citigroup's (C.N) Michael Corbat, Wells Fargo's John Stumpf (WFC.N) and TD Bank's Bharat Masrani (TD.TO) all left their respective CEO roles after running into similarly significant regulatory problems. President Donald Trump's vexing track record, however, probably gives Moynihan extra wiggle room. It's easy to question the motivations here. For one thing, Trump [USN:FWN3W42W4 TEXT:"pardoned"] Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who had pleaded guilty to anti-money-laundering violations and stepped down from the cryptocurrency exchange as part of a $4.3 billion settlement. Administration officials also have been echoing industry complaints that suspicious-activity reporting rules have become overly burdensome. Dubious probes like the one into former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell have more than a whiff of political bullying. Moreover, just days into his second term, the president publicly [USN:S0N3OG012 TEXT:"rebuked"] Moynihan at the World Economic Forum in Davos for allegedly discriminating against conservative customers. Moynihan is under some justified pressure. BofA's share price gains have broadly under-performed the industry in recent years, prompting investors to push him to boost returns on tangible common equity into the high teens, even as some rivals already exceed 20%. The bank recently tried to [USN:L1N45V0WY TEXT:"reassure"] staff about deal-maker defections, Reuters reported this week. Even excluding the latest regulatory penalty, its third-quarter earnings would have declined, making it an outlier among large lenders. Although compliance shortcomings add to the CEO's challenges, the true extent of the problem is hard to discern because of who's shouting about them. As a result, Moynihan has scope to keep the real wolves at bay. Follow Stephen Gandel on LinkedIn and X . Bank of America on October 13 agreed to pay a $1.2 billion fine to settle accusations in a civil case brought by the financial crimes unit of the Treasury Department and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency that it failed to address previously flagged lapses in its anti-money-laundering controls. The US regulators said the bank failed to report in a timely way more than $5 billion of suspicious transactions to Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. As part of the settlement, BofA admits that it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act and failed to implement and maintain an anti-money-laundering program that met minimum regulatory requirements, Treasury said in a statement. BofA is required to work with a third party to identify and report suspicious transactions that were undetected and undergo an independent review of its suspicious activity monitoring and other programs, according to the consent order. item.title: Britons have not been told to start wearing face masks again
item.description: The UK Health Security Agency says its advice on face masks remains unchanged despite online posts suggesting Britons have been newly advised to start wearing them.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Fact Check
item.content:encoded: The UK Health Security Agency says its advice on face masks remains unchanged despite online posts suggesting Britons have been newly advised to start wearing them. The Liverpool Echo newspaper posted an image on Facebook carrying the headline, "People advised to start wearing masks again." The text of its October 11 post clarified that the UKHSA advised masks for people with COVID-19 symptoms who were unable to isolate at home and as of October 14, the post has the changed headline, “Advice issued as winter viruses rise.” But other social media posts reshared the original headline without its context. Comments underneath the posts suggested some people thought the headline referred to new advice about face mask restrictions affecting everyone. "I wouldn't be too surprised if this latest round of scaremongering and bullshit fizzles out in about a month much like a faulty firework on November 5th," one comment said . Another said : "What a load of scaremongering rubbish again. I will not be doing lockdown again. No mask. No staying in. No ridiculousness!" However, a spokesperson for UKHSA said in an email its guidance remains unchanged and that if you have COVID you should consider wearing a mask if you are unable to stay at home. An October 8 UKHSA blog post reporting a 7% rise in positive COVID test results also referred to existing guidance for people with respiratory virus symptoms to stay home if possible, and if not, to wear a mask to avoid infecting others. The same guidance has been available on the government's website since at least April 1, 2022, according to an archived webpage . The agency also advises people to consider wearing a face mask if they come into close contact with someone at high risk of becoming seriously unwell with COVID or when rates of COVID or other respiratory illnesses are high. There is no evidence the UK government has issued new advice that the wider population should wear face masks again. A spokesperson for the Liverpool Echo said in an email: "We felt the UKHSA sharing their advice again recently, even if it was unchanged, did merit a news story to share this important health advice widely. "The graphic which has been shared without context elsewhere was taken from a Facebook post in which it was accompanied by the full UKHSA statement and our full story. "The graphic could have been more clear that the guidance applied only to some people, and on being alerted to the issue by the UKHSA on Monday we replaced the graphic immediately." The National Health Service did not respond to a request for comment. VERDICT Misleading. The UKHSA has repromoted existing advice about wearing face masks if you have COVID, not told the general population to start wearing masks again. item.title: Mega-IPOs broaden appeal of tycoon wealth tactics
item.description: Private companies like Anthropic have many millionaires on paper. Yet workers can’t cash out at will, while selling incurs taxes and forgoes potential upside. With large unlisted firms worth some $5.3 trln, employee borrowing against stock could move beyond corner offices.
item.dc:creator: Pranav Kiran
item.content:encoded: Mega initial public offerings like Anthropic may create a new class of everyday millionaires. Unlike boss Dario Amodei, however, employees often have no easy way to tap that wealth before the day their company floats. Selling shares sacrifices upside and incurs taxes. Borrowing against equity, a staple of private banking, could become another way to unlock a pool of stock-based pay. There is a wide gap between the glamor and reality of stock-based pay. Sure, graffiti artist David Choe was paid in stock for painting Facebook’s office and turned millionaire when the company now known as Meta Platforms (META.O) went public. But most startup employees don't work at unicorns, Silicon Valley slang for private companies worth over $1 billion. The median employee is more likely to see a low five-figure payout, and their firm sold for less than $100 million, Nick Maggiulli , chief operating officer at wealth management firm Ritholtz, reckons. Unicorn exits can generate life-changing wealth. But higher interest rates and lower relative valuations on public markets mean there's a backlog of giant private firms that can't, or won't, go public. These are now worth $5.3 trillion in aggregate, PitchBook data shows. Eager venture investors and control-hungry founders have meanwhile pushed the median age of companies going public to 14 years, according to University of Florida’s Jay Ritter. Companies have turned to private market deals. Hotly anticipated IPO candidates like Databricks and OpenAI are increasingly running tender offers to buy back some employee shares. Such deals executed on Nasdaq Private Market rose from about $3 billion in 2023 to just under $15 billion in 2025. Borrowing against that stock is another method. This offers employees liquidity, without the need to wait for an IPO or give up potential future gains. Such services though have been reserved for ultra wealthy clients with large portfolios and other assets to pledge as collateral. Yet, the pool of potential borrowers is expanding. Employees typically own a larger chunk of stock than founders by the time a startup hits a Series C funding round, according to Carta. That prospect has spawned upstarts like Techdollar . Secfi, which operates as an asset manager, has facilitated about $1 billion in financing for private startup shareholders against their holdings. Stocks now make up more than a third of US households’ net worth. For private startup employees, this can be as high as 86%, according to Secfi data. Borrowing against it could become less niche. item.content:encoded: Les craintes sur la dette liée à l'IA bousculent à nouveau les Bourses mondiales 15 octobre (Reuters) - Wall Street est attendue en ordre dispersé et les Bourses européennes évoluent également dans le désordre jeudi à mi-séance, les inquiétudes sur le niveau d'endettement des entreprises liées à l'intelligence artificielle (IA) refaisant surface et poussant les investisseurs vers les valeurs refuge. Les futures sur indices new-yorkais signalent une ouverture en hausse de 0,26% pour le Dow Jones, mais en baisse de 0,29% pour le Standard & Poor's-500 et de 1,22% pour le Nasdaq. TSMC-Bénéfice record pour le sixième trimestre consécutif grâce à l'IA 15 octobre (Reuters) - Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) a affiché jeudi un sixième trimestre consécutif de résultats records, porté par l'essor des dépenses d'infrastructure dans le secteur technologique. GB: Une hausse des taux n'est pas nécessairement le début d'une longue série, selon Pill (BoE) BANGKOK, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Un possible relèvement des taux directeurs par la Banque d'Angleterre (BoE) ne doit pas être interprétée par les investisseurs comme le début d'une longue série de hausses, a déclaré jeudi Huw Pill, chef économiste de l'institut d'émission monétaire britannique. Zone euro: L'inflation énergétique ne s'étend pas sur le reste des prix, selon Pereira (BCE) BANGKOK, 15 octobre (Reuters) - L'inflation liée aux prix de l'énergie dans la zone euro ne se répercute pas sur les autres prix, ce qui constitue un signe rassurant pour la Banque centrale européenne (BCE), a déclaré jeudi Alvaro Santos Pereira, membre du conseil des gouverneurs de l'institution de Francfort et gouverneur de la banque centrale du Portugal. Ericsson: Le bénéfice baisse moins que prévu au T3, malgré la hausse des coûts des composants STOCKHOLM, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le fabricant suédois d'équipements de télécommunications Ericsson a annoncé jeudi une baisse de son résultat opérationnel au troisième trimestre moins importante que prévu, tout en avertissant que la hausse des coûts des composants pèserait sur les marges l'année prochaine. France: L'inflation IPCH accélère comme prévu à +3,4% sur un an en septembre 15 octobre (Reuters) - L'inflation en France, harmonisée selon les normes européennes (IPCH), a accéléré comme attendu à +3,4% sur un an en septembre, montrent les données définitives publiées jeudi par l'Insee.

item.content:encoded: Le sommet UE-Golfe prévu le 24/10 à Ryad est reporté RYAD/BRUXELLES, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le sommet prévu le 24 octobre à Ryad entre l'Union européenne et le Conseil de coopération du Golfe (CCG) a été reporté jeudi pour des raisons de sécurité, en raison notamment des attaques répétées des Houthis contre l'Arabie saoudite qui perturbent le trafic aérien. Moscou construit une base de lancement de drones à réaction en un temps record LONDRES, 15 octobre (Reuters) - La Russie a quasiment achevé la construction d'une nouvelle base destinée au lancement de drones à réaction en à peine six semaines, selon des experts de la défense et une analyse de Reuters fondée sur des images satellites, dernier exemple de l'expansion de ses capacités de frappe à proximité de l'Ukraine. Le réseau Starshield rétabli en Ukraine, selon une source KYIV, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le réseau de satellites à usage militaire Starshield, développé par SpaceX, a été pleinement rétabli en Ukraine, a déclaré jeudi une source au sein du ministère ukrainien de la Défense, au lendemain de restrictions imposées à ce service essentiel aux forces de Kyiv. Le toit d'une école s'effondre au Pakistan, 32 enfants tués ISLAMABAD, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Trente-deux enfants ainsi qu'une enseignante ont été tués jeudi au Pakistan par l'effondrement du toit de leur école à Peshawar, rapportent la police et les secours. L'Europe incapable de suppléer aux dysfonctionnements de Starlink en Ukraine 15 octobre (Reuters) - A cours d'une semaine où l'Ukraine a dû faire face à des restrictions du réseau satellitaire Starlink et à l'absence de données américaines la renseignant de l'imminence de frappes de missiles balistiques russes, Kyiv se rend à l'évidence que l'Europe n'est pas en mesure d'offrir la moindre alternative. Roumanie: Deux bateaux en feu en mer Noire, huit portés disparus BUCHAREST, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Des équipes de secours roumaines sont à la recherche de huit membres d'équipage d'un chimiquier qui a pris feu jeudi dans les eaux territoriales de la Roumanie en mer Noire, incident qui coïncide avec la détection d'une présence de drones russes dans l'espace aérien roumain, ont dit les autorités du pays. La marine ukrainienne dit avoir endommagé six avions de combat russes 15 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée ukrainienne a affirmé jeudi avoir endommagé à des degrés divers six chasseurs-bombardiers russes Su-34M lors d'une frappe nocturne sur l'aérodrome de Borissoglebsk, dans la région russe de Voronej. Les Etats-Unis envisagent d'alléger les sanctions contre la "flotte fantôme", selon un responsable WASHINGTON, 14 octobre (Reuters) - L'administration américaine envisage d'alléger les sanctions contre les navires de la "flotte fantôme", qui transportent notamment du pétrole en provenance de pays comme la Russie, l'Iran ou le Venezuela, afin de faire baisser les taux de fret mondiaux, qui ont atteint des niveaux records, a dit mercredi un responsable américain. Le Sénat brésilien approuve la réduction du temps de travail, mesure portée par Lula SÃO PAULO, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le Sénat brésilien a approuvé mercredi soir un amendement constitutionnel visant à réduire la semaine de travail de six à cinq jours, offrant ainsi au président Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva une victoire législative à moins de deux semaines du second tour de l'élection présidentielle qui s'annonce serré pour lui. L'armée américaine envisage d'utiliser la "mère de toutes les bombes" en Iran, selon CNN 15 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée américaine a développé des plans de frappes qui pourraient inclure l'utilisation de la bombe GBU-43, la bombe conventionnelle la plus puissante jamais utilisée en zone de combats par l'armée américaine, en Iran si Donald Trump décidait de la reprise des hostilités, rapporte jeudi CNN, citant des responsables américains au fait de la question.
